image.altEn: Spanish-language xkcd comic #505: A Bunch of Rocks

titleText.es: Invoco la regla 34 sobre la regla 34 de Wolfram.
titleText.en: I call Rule 34 on Wolfram's Rule 34.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive closely renders the official title text. The joke crosses the internet adage commonly called Rule 34 with Stephen Wolfram's numbered cellular-automaton Rule 34; it does not claim that Wolfram's Rule 34 is the Turing-complete system shown in the image. No source-number or title-text anomaly was found.

regions.labelEs: ASÍ QUE ESTOY ATRAPADO EN ESTE DESIERTO POR TODA LA ETERNIDAD.

applications.explanationEn: Así que introduces the result that follows.
Estoy presents the speaker's current state, and atrapado is the masculine singular completed-action form describing the result of being trapped.

regions.labelEs: NO SÉ POR QUÉ. SIMPLEMENTE ME DESPERTÉ AQUÍ UN DÍA.

applications.explanationEn: The two written words por qué ask for a reason, and qué carries a written accent.
Simple has the same masculine and feminine singular form, so adding -mente produces simplemente.
Desperté presents waking up as one completed past event.

regions.labelEs: NUNCA SIENTO NI HAMBRE NI SED.

applications.explanationEn: The two copies of ni place hambre and sed inside the same paired negative.

regions.labelEs: SOLO CAMINO.
ARENA Y ROCAS
HASTA EL INFINITO. HASTA DONDE YO SÉ.

applications.explanationEn: Hasta donde sets the boundary of the speaker's knowledge, and yo sé names that speaker's knowledge explicitly.

regions.labelEs: AQUÍ HAY MUCHO TIEMPO PARA PENSAR. UNA ETERNIDAD, DE HECHO.

applications.explanationEn: Hay tiempo para supplies the availability pattern, mucho measures the available time, and pensar names the action in its unchanged dictionary form.
The fixed connector de hecho sharpens the preceding claim with a confirming fact.

regions.labelEs: RECONSTRUÍ LA MATEMÁTICA MODERNA EN LA ARENA Y LA AMPLIÉ.

applications.explanationEn: Reconstruí presents the reconstruction as a completed past event.
Matemática names the field first, and moderna follows it as the neutral description.
Moderna uses feminine singular -a because it describes the feminine singular noun matemática.
La replaces the already named feminine subject matter and appears immediately before the changed verb amplié.
Amplié presents the expansion as a completed past event.

regions.labelEs: LA FÍSICA TAMBIÉN. PULÍ ALGUNOS FLECOS EN LA MECÁNICA CUÁNTICA Y LA RELATIVIDAD. ME COSTÓ BASTANTE, PERO ESTE SITIO TIENE MENOS DISTRACCIONES QUE UNA OFICINA DE PATENTES SUIZA.

applications.explanationEn: Mecánica names the field first, and cuántica follows it as the neutral description.
Cuántica uses feminine singular -a because it describes the feminine singular noun mecánica.
Oficina de patentes names the institution first, and suiza follows it as the neutral nationality description.
Suiza is feminine singular because it describes oficina, not the intervening plural noun patentes.
Pulí supplies the completed polishing action, algunos measures the remaining details, and flecos carries the figurative loose-ends sense.
Pulí presents the refining as a completed past event.
Costó presents the experienced difficulty as a bounded past event.

regions.labelEs: UN DÍA EMPECÉ A COLOCAR FILAS DE PIEDRAS.

applications.explanationEn: Empecé changes for the speaker and completed past, a links to the action, and colocar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Empecé presents the beginning as one completed point in the past.

regions.labelEs: CADA FILA SEGUÍA A LA ANTERIOR EN UN PATRÓN SIMPLE.

applications.explanationEn: La and anterior remain feminine singular because they stand for the already mentioned fila without repeating that noun.
Patrón names the pattern first, and simple follows it as the neutral description.
Simple stays singular to match patrón; this adjective has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns.
Seguía uses the imperfect because the repeated row-to-row relationship is continuing background.

regions.labelEs: CON LAS REGLAS ADECUADAS Y SUFICIENTE ESPACIO,

applications.explanationEn: Reglas names the things first, and adecuadas follows as their neutral description.
Adecuadas uses feminine plural -as because it describes the feminine plural noun reglas.

regions.labelEs: FUI CAPAZ DE CONSTRUIR UN ORDENADOR. CADA NUEVA FILA DE PIEDRAS ES LA SIGUIENTE ITERACIÓN DE LA COMPUTACIÓN.

applications.explanationEn: Nueva uses feminine singular -a because it describes the feminine singular noun fila.
Fui changes ser for the speaker and past, capaz de supplies the ability pattern, and construir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Fui presents the achieved state as bounded in the past.

regions.labelEs: SÍ, USA ROCAS EN VEZ DE ELECTRICIDAD, PERO ES LO MISMO*. SÓLO QUE MÁS LENTO.

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed asterisk points to the footnote below and is not a Spanish lexical word.

applications.explanationEn: Neutral lo turns mismo into the abstract idea ‘the same thing’ without naming a masculine noun.
En vez de introduces the replacement, and electricidad fills the noun slot for what is replaced.
Sólo que introduces the limiting contrast, and más lento supplies the qualification.

regions.labelEs: * TURING-COMPLETO

excludedUnits.rationale: This asterisk marks the explanatory footnote and is not a Spanish lexical word.
Turing is the proper surname in the international technical term, not a Spanish vocabulary word.

regions.labelEs: TRAS UN RATO LO PROGRAMÉ COMO SIMULADOR FÍSICO.

applications.explanationEn: Simulador names the device or program first, and físico follows it as the neutral description.
Físico uses masculine singular -o because it describes the masculine singular noun simulador.
Lo replaces the already understood computer and appears immediately before the changed verb programé.
Programé presents the programming as a completed past event.

regions.labelEs: TODA LA INFORMACIÓN DE UNA PARTÍCULA SE CODIFICABA COMO UNA CADENA DE BITS ESCRITA EN LAS PIEDRAS. 00101010 00101010

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed binary data string encodes a value and is not a Spanish lexical word.
This second printed binary data string is another encoded value, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Cadena de bits names the thing first, and escrita follows it as the neutral description.
Escrita is feminine singular because it describes cadena, not the intervening masculine plural noun bits.
Se leaves the person doing the encoding unnamed, while codificaba supplies the ongoing past encoding action.
Codificaba uses the imperfect because it describes the encoding method as continuing background.

regions.labelEs: CON SUFICIENTE TIEMPO Y ESPACIO, PUDE SIMULAR COMPLETAMENTE LA INTERACCIÓN DE DOS PARTÍCULAS.

applications.explanationEn: Completa is the feminine singular form of completo; adding -mente produces completamente.
Pude changes poder for the speaker and completed past, while simular stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Pude presents the successful ability as a completed past event.

regions.labelEs: PERO TENGO TIEMPO Y ESPACIO INFINITOS.

applications.explanationEn: Infinitos is masculine plural because it describes two masculine singular nouns together: tiempo and espacio.

regions.labelEs: ASÍ QUE DECIDÍ SIMULAR UN UNIVERSO.

applications.explanationEn: Así que introduces the resulting decision.
Decidí presents the decision as a completed past event.

regions.labelEs: PASAN EONES MIENTRAS RECORRO UNA FILA.
LAS FILAS SE SUCEDEN PARA COMPUTAR CADA ITERACIÓN.

applications.explanationEn: Para introduces the purpose, and computar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: Y EN LA SIMULACIÓN
TRANSCURRE OTRO INSTANTE.
ASÍ QUE SI VES DESAPARECER UNA MOTA DE POLVO EN UN PEQUEÑO FLASH O ALGO ASÍ

applications.explanationEn: The borrowed noun flash is treated as masculine singular here, so the describing word takes the matching form pequeño.
Así que introduces the resulting condition that follows.

applications.exampleEs: VES DESAPARECER UNA MOTA DE POLVO
applications.explanationEn: Ves changes ver for one familiar viewer, desaparecer stays in its unchanged dictionary form, and una mota de polvo names the thing observed performing that action.
The fixed phrase o algo así marks the preceding description as approximate.

regions.labelEs: LO SIENTO. DEBO HABERME EQUIVOCADO CON UNA ROCA EN ALGÚN MOMENTO DE LOS ÚLTIMOS BILLONES Y BILLONES DE MILENIOS.

applications.explanationEn: Lo siento is the fixed two-word apology.
Debo marks a strong conclusion, haberme supplies the perfect helper with me attached, and equivocado is the completed-action form.
Haberme supplies unchanged haber with me attached, and equivocado supplies the completed-action form.
Me attaches to the end of the unchanged verb form haber.
This occurrence renders the official English source's “billions.” Standard Spanish billones normally denotes groups of 10¹², so the archive wording changes the conventional scale.
This repeated occurrence again renders official English “billions”; standard Spanish normally uses billones for groups of 10¹².

regions.labelEs: AH, Y...
SI PENSABAS QUE LOS MINUTOS DE TU CLASE MATUTINA TE RESULTABAN DEMASIADO LENTOS...

applications.explanationEn: Pensabas uses the imperfect because it presents a continuing past viewpoint or assumption.

applications.exampleEs: LOS MINUTOS DE TU CLASE MATUTINA TE RESULTABAN DEMASIADO LENTOS
applications.explanationEn: Los minutos de tu clase matutina supplies the plural thing judged, te names the person experiencing the impression, resultaban agrees with that plural subject in the past, and demasiado lentos supplies the resulting description.
Resultaban uses the imperfect because it presents a continuing past impression rather than one bounded event.
Clase names the thing first, and the neutral descriptive adjective matutina follows it.
Matutina uses feminine singular -a because it describes the feminine singular noun clase.

applications.exampleEs: MINUTOS DE TU CLASE MATUTINA TE RESULTABAN DEMASIADO LENTOS
applications.explanationEn: Lentos uses masculine plural -os because it describes the masculine plural noun minutos.

cards.answerEn: so; therefore (as part of así que)

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a situation to its result with “so”?
cards.answerEn: Use así que before the result.
cards.noteEn: Así que joins a cause or situation to what follows from it. The two words work together as one connector; translating así and que separately will not give the intended meaning.

example.es: Está lloviendo, así que llevo un paraguas.
example.en: It is raining, so I am carrying an umbrella.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a result connector
I am (in a state or condition)

cards.promptEs: estar + forma de acción completada que describe un estado
cards.questionEn: How do you describe the state something is in as the result of an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by the action's completed form, with an ending that matches the thing being described.
cards.noteEn: The completed form, often ending in -ado or -ido, is also called a participle. Estar changes for who or what is in the state. The participle changes like a describing word: cerrado, cerrada, cerrados, or cerradas. This pattern focuses on the resulting state, not on who performed the action.

example.en: The doors are closed.

cards.noteEn: Atrapado can describe someone unable to leave a place or situation. The ending changes to match the person or thing described: atrapado, atrapada, atrapados, or atrapadas.

example.es: El coche quedó atrapado en la nieve.
example.en: The car got stuck in the snow.

cards.noteEn: Por can present a period as the span through which a situation lasts. This is different from para when para points toward a purpose or intended deadline.

example.en: They lived there for many years.

cards.noteEn: Una eternidad often exaggerates how long something feels rather than literally claiming that it never ends.

example.en: The wait felt like an eternity.

cards.noteEn: Write the question form as two words, with an accent on qué. Write the usual answer word porque as one word without an accent.
cards.questionEn: How do you write “why” and “because” in Spanish?

example.es: ¿Por qué estudias español? Porque me gusta.
example.en: Why do you study Spanish? Because I like it.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

example.en: Lucía answers clearly.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

example.en: I complain about the noise.

cards.noteEn: Desperté is the completed-past form of despertar used for yo. When it describes waking up rather than waking someone else, Spanish normally uses it with me: me desperté.

example.en: I woke up early.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.answerEn: one; a certain (before a masculine time word)
cards.noteEn: Before a masculine time word, un can point to one unspecified occasion rather than simply serving as the article “a.”

example.en: One day I will return to Granada.

cards.noteEn: Siento is the form of sentir used by the speaker. With me before it, me siento describes how the speaker feels or what the speaker feels like; this is different from lo siento, the fixed expression for “I'm sorry.”

example.en: I feel better today.

cards.noteEn: Repeated ni places each item inside the same negative choice: ni X ni Y. English commonly renders the pair as “neither X nor Y.”

example.es: No quiero ni té ni café.
example.en: I want neither tea nor coffee.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “neither this nor that” in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Put ni before each rejected item: ni X ni Y.
cards.noteEn: The plus signs show the order of the pieces, and X and Y stand for the two items. After a negative verb, repeated ni keeps both items inside that negation. Without an earlier verb, ni X ni Y can itself begin a negative statement.

example.es: No tengo ni tiempo ni dinero.
example.en: I have neither time nor money.

cards.noteEn: Camino is the present form of caminar used for yo. The same spelling can also be the noun camino, “path” or “way,” but that is a different sense.

example.en: I walk to the station.

cards.promptEs: filas de piedras como ordenador Turing-completo
cards.questionEn: How can rows of rocks updated by simple rules act like a computer?
cards.answerEn: They form a cellular automaton: each new row is calculated from the previous row, and a suitable rule system can perform general computation.
cards.noteEn: A cellular automaton is a grid of simple cells updated in steps by local rules. One row can encode the current state and the next row the following step. Turing-complete means capable in principle of carrying out any general computation when given enough time and storage. The title separately puns on Wolfram's numbered Rule 34 and the internet adage commonly called Rule 34; it does not establish that Wolfram's Rule 34 is itself the universal system being described.
Before a place, hasta marks the endpoint reached by movement. English often uses simply to, while as far as makes the endpoint emphasis explicit.

example.en: We walked to the station.

cards.answerEn: as far as (setting a limit on knowledge)
cards.noteEn: In hasta donde alguien sabe, hasta marks the boundary of that person's knowledge rather than a physical destination.

example.es: Hasta donde sé, la tienda abre hoy.
example.en: As far as I know, the store opens today.

cards.questionEn: How do you limit a statement to what you currently know?
cards.answerEn: Use hasta donde yo sé to mean “as far as I know.”
cards.noteEn: Hasta sets a boundary, donde marks where that boundary lies, and yo sé states whose knowledge is limited. The subject word can change or be omitted: hasta donde sabemos means “as far as we know,” and hasta donde sé keeps the same meaning without yo.

example.es: Hasta donde yo sé, Ana llega mañana.
example.en: As far as I know, Ana arrives tomorrow.

cards.answerEn: where; as far as (in hasta donde)
cards.noteEn: After hasta, donde identifies the figurative boundary reached by someone's knowledge. It has no written accent because it is not asking a question.

example.en: As far as we know, everything works.

cards.promptEs: hay tiempo para + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that there is time available to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use hay tiempo para, then put the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Hay says that something exists and does not change for one thing or several. Tiempo names the available time, and para introduces its use. The following action stays in its dictionary form, the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Other times can use había tiempo or habrá tiempo.

example.en: There is time to rest.

cards.noteEn: After tiempo, para introduces the action for which time is available. The action verb then stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: There is time to eat.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de hecho, ‘in fact’

cards.questionEn: How do you add a fact that confirms or sharpens what you just said?
cards.answerEn: Use de hecho for “in fact” or “actually.”
cards.noteEn: De hecho is a fixed connector. It introduces a fact that supports, corrects, or makes the preceding point more precise; the individual words do not need to be translated separately.

example.es: No está lejos; de hecho, podemos ir andando.
example.en: It is not far; in fact, we can walk there.

cards.noteEn: Reconstruí is the completed-past form of reconstruir used for yo. The written accent marks the stressed final sound.

example.en: I rebuilt the old table.

cards.noteEn: The singular matemática can name mathematics as a field. The plural matemáticas is also very common for the subject or activity.

example.en: Mathematics studies patterns.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

example.en: The movie—we watched it yesterday.

cards.noteEn: Amplié is the completed-past form of ampliar used for yo. The written accent keeps the final syllable stressed.

example.en: I expanded the garden.

cards.noteEn: Pulí is the completed-past form of pulir used for yo. It can describe making a surface smooth or refining details in a plan or piece of work.

example.en: I polished the details of the report.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone refines the remaining loose ends of some work?
cards.answerEn: Use pulir los flecos de algo for polishing or ironing out its remaining details.
cards.noteEn: Pulir literally means to polish a surface. Flecos are literally fringes or dangling edges, but figuratively they are small details still needing attention. Pulir changes for the person and time; the article or quantity before flecos can vary.

example.es: Pulimos los últimos flecos del proyecto.
example.en: We polished the project's remaining loose ends.

cards.noteEn: A fleco is literally a fringe or dangling edge. In work that is almost finished, plural flecos can figuratively mean small details still needing attention.

example.en: A few loose ends remain to be resolved.

cards.answerEn: quantum; relating to quantum physics (feminine singular)
cards.noteEn: Cuántica describes a feminine singular noun in the context of quantum physics. The masculine singular form is cuántico.

example.en: They study quantum physics.

cards.promptEs: Einstein, la relatividad y la oficina de patentes suiza
cards.questionEn: Why does a Swiss patent office belong in a joke about developing relativity?
cards.answerEn: Albert Einstein worked at the Swiss Federal Patent Office in Bern while developing the ideas behind special relativity.
cards.noteEn: Einstein held the patent-office job from 1902 to 1909 and published his special-relativity paper in 1905. References to relativity, a patent office, and Switzerland therefore point to that famous part of his biography.

cards.answerEn: for me; marks me as the person who finds something difficult
cards.noteEn: With costar in the sense “to be difficult,” me identifies the person who experiences the difficulty. Spanish makes the difficult task the grammatical subject.

example.en: It was hard for me to understand the question.

cards.noteEn: Costó is a completed-past form of costar. With me, te, le, nos, os, or les, it can describe how difficult something was for that person rather than its price.

example.en: It was hard for us to finish on time.

cards.noteEn: After an action verb, bastante can strengthen the amount or degree of that action. This differs from bastante before a noun, where it can mean “enough.”

example.en: The trip lasted quite a while.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

example.en: I need a coffee cup.

cards.noteEn: Empecé is the completed-past form of empezar used for yo. The spelling changes from z to c before é so the consonant sound stays the same.

example.en: I started reading yesterday.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone starts doing an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of empezar, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” The dictionary form, also called the infinitive, is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Empezar changes for the person and time; a stays fixed, and the action verb stays unchanged.

example.en: Lucía starts to read.

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)

cards.noteEn: Seguía is an imperfect past form of seguir used for one subject. The imperfect presents the repeated row-to-row relationship as ongoing background rather than one completed event.

example.en: Each chapter followed the previous one.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word in this use; required before what is followed
cards.noteEn: Seguir a alguien or algo can mean to follow that person or thing in a sequence. English does not place a separate preposition before the target.

example.en: Tuesday follows Monday.

cards.promptEs: el/la/los/las o un/una + adjetivo sin repetir el sustantivo
cards.questionEn: How do you say “the interesting one” or “a small one” without repeating the noun?
cards.answerEn: Keep the article and adjective, omit the repeated noun, and make both agree with that understood noun.
cards.noteEn: The article is a word such as el, la, un, or una. The adjective still changes to match the omitted noun: una pequeña can mean “a small feminine one,” while uno pequeño can mean “a small masculine one.” Context supplies the missing noun.

example.es: Quiero una taza; dame la pequeña.
example.en: I want a cup; give me the small one.

cards.noteEn: Anterior can stand on its own when the omitted noun is already clear. The article la shows that the understood noun is feminine singular.

example.es: Esta página es más clara que la anterior.
example.en: This page is clearer than the previous one.

cards.noteEn: Suficiente describes an adequate amount or degree. After neutral lo, lo suficiente means “enough” or “what is sufficient.”

example.en: That is enough.

cards.noteEn: Fui is the irregular completed-past form of ser used for yo. The same form can also be the completed past of ir, “I went”; context distinguishes them.

example.en: I was able to solve it.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is able to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ser, then capaz de, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form, also called the infinitive, is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Ser changes for the person and time, and capaz becomes capaces for more than one person. Keep de before the final action verb, which remains unchanged.

example.en: Lucía is able to swim.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; a required verb complement
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs require de before their complement or a following infinitive. English often absorbs this de into the verb’s translation: dejar de means “to stop doing,” while disfrutar de means “to enjoy.”

example.en: I stopped smoking.

cards.noteEn: Usa is the present form of usar used for one third-person subject. It can also be an informal positive command meaning “use,” but that is not this sense.

example.en: The machine uses little energy.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en vez de, ‘instead of’
cards.noteEn: En belongs to the fixed three-word connector en vez de. Learn the connector as a unit rather than translating en as ordinary ‘in.’

example.es: Tomé té en vez de café.
example.en: I had tea instead of coffee.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one option replaces another?
cards.answerEn: Put en vez de before the alternative that was not chosen: ‘instead of.’
cards.noteEn: A noun, pronoun, or unchanged action verb can follow: en vez de café, en vez de eso, en vez de llamar. The three words en vez de stay together.

example.es: Usamos el tren en vez del coche.
example.en: We used the train instead of the car.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; forms en vez de, ‘instead of’
cards.noteEn: Vez often means an occurrence or time, but inside en vez de it helps form the fixed connector ‘instead of.’

example.es: Fuimos andando en vez de tomar el autobús.
example.en: We walked instead of taking the bus.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes en vez de, ‘instead of’
cards.noteEn: De finishes the connector en vez de and comes directly before the alternative that is not chosen.

example.es: Escribió un correo en vez de llamar.
example.en: She wrote an email instead of calling.

cards.answerEn: the (neutral article before an adjective, as in lo mejor)
cards.noteEn: Neutral lo turns an adjective into an abstract idea: lo importante means “the important thing,” not a masculine noun.

example.en: The important thing is to begin.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to “what is important,” “the difficult part,” or another general quality without naming a noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the unchanged word lo before a masculine-singular adjective: lo importante, lo difícil, lo bueno.
cards.noteEn: Here lo does not stand for a masculine object. It turns the quality into a general idea or aspect, such as lo importante, “what is important.” The adjective stays in its masculine singular form because there is no named noun for it to match.

example.en: The difficult part is starting.

cards.noteEn: The comic uses the formerly common accent in sólo. Current standard spelling normally writes solo without an accent when it means “only,” unless an accent is exceptionally needed to prevent genuine ambiguity.

example.en: I only need a minute.

cards.questionEn: How do you add a limiting contrast, like “except that” or “only ...”?
cards.answerEn: Use solo que, then state the qualification or contrast.
cards.noteEn: Solo que preserves the main idea but adds one important limitation. Some texts write sólo with an accent in this adverbial use; current standard spelling normally omits the accent unless it is needed to prevent ambiguity.

example.es: La ruta funciona, solo que tarda más.
example.en: The route works, except that it takes longer.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes solo que, ‘except that’
complete; capable of general computation (in Turing-completo)
cards.noteEn: In the technical expression Turing-completo, completo means that a system can in principle carry out any computation that a general-purpose computer can, given enough time and storage. Completo agrees with a masculine singular system.

example.en: That language is Turing-complete.

cards.answerEn: while; a short or unspecified period of time
cards.noteEn: Un rato refers to an imprecise stretch of time. Its length depends on the situation rather than on a fixed number of minutes.

example.en: We rest for a while.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.noteEn: Programé is the completed-past form of programar used for yo. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

example.en: I programmed a small tool.

cards.answerEn: as (in the role or capacity of)
cards.noteEn: Unaccented como can introduce the role, identity, or point of view from which someone speaks or acts. This is different from cómo with an accent, which asks “how.”

example.en: As a doctor, I recommend resting.

cards.noteEn: Físico can describe something related to physics or the physical world. As a noun, físico can instead mean “physicist.”

example.en: They built a physical model.

cards.answerEn: marks an action whose doer is not named
cards.noteEn: Before a third-person verb, se can focus on what happens rather than who does it. English often uses a passive form such as ‘is requested’ or ‘have been discovered.’

example.en: Several errors were found.

cards.promptEs: se + verbo en tercera persona (sin nombrar quién actúa)
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish focus on an action or result without naming who does it?
cards.answerEn: Put se before a third-person verb and state what happens; the person doing it can remain unnamed.
cards.noteEn: English often uses a passive form. Spanish may use se with a simple verb or with a completed construction such as se han encontrado. Other uses of se follow different patterns.

example.en: The results were published.

cards.answerEn: was encoded; used to be encoded (with se)
cards.noteEn: Codificaba is an imperfect past form of codificar. With se before it, the thing being encoded is presented as the subject and the encoder is left unnamed.

example.es: El mensaje se codificaba en números.
example.en: The message was encoded as numbers.

cards.noteEn: In computing, cadena is a sequence of characters or bits; outside computing it can mean a physical chain.

example.es: El programa lee una cadena de letras.
example.en: The program reads a string of letters.

cards.noteEn: Escrita is the completed-action form of escribir and takes the feminine singular ending when it describes a feminine singular noun.

example.es: La nota está escrita a mano.
example.en: The note is written by hand.

cards.answerEn: I was able to; I managed to
cards.noteEn: Pude is the irregular completed-past form of poder used for yo. Before an unchanged action verb, it often says that the speaker succeeded in doing that action.

example.en: I managed to finish the work.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

example.en: We can enter now.

cards.noteEn: Decidí is the completed-past form of decidir used for yo. It can be followed directly by an unchanged action verb.

example.en: I decided to wait.

cards.answerEn: they pass; they go by (time periods)
cards.noteEn: When the subject is a plural span of time, pasar describes that time elapsing. Pasan is the present form used for a plural subject.

example.en: The years go by quickly.

cards.noteEn: Recorro is the present form of recorrer used for yo. It describes covering or moving along the length of a route, area, or sequence.

example.en: I go along the path every morning.

cards.answerEn: one another; marks sucederse, ‘to follow one another’
cards.noteEn: With a plural subject, se suceden presents repeated events or items as following one another in sequence.

example.es: Los días se suceden sin pausa.
example.en: The days follow one another without pause.

cards.answerEn: follow one another; occur in succession (with se)
cards.noteEn: Suceden is the present plural form of suceder. With se, it describes things coming one after another.

example.en: The meetings follow one another quickly.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.noteEn: Transcurre is the present form of transcurrir used for one subject, often a period or moment of time.

example.en: The afternoon passes quietly.

cards.promptEs: ver + persona o cosa + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that you see a person or thing perform an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ver, name the person or thing observed, and put the observed action in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The plus signs show the order of the pieces. The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Only ver changes for the viewer and time. A specific person normally takes a before them: veo a Marta correr. The observed person or thing can also follow the action verb, especially when it is new information.

example.en: I see Marta run.

cards.noteEn: Flash is a borrowed English noun commonly used in Spanish for a brief burst of light. This is different from Flash as the name of Adobe's former multimedia platform.

example.es: Vimos un flash en el cielo.
example.en: We saw a flash in the sky.

cards.questionEn: How do you soften an estimate by saying “or something like that”?
cards.answerEn: Add o algo así after an approximate description.
cards.noteEn: O introduces an alternative, algo means an unspecified thing, and así means “like that.” Together they signal that the preceding description is only approximate.

example.es: Llegará el martes o algo así.
example.en: He or she will arrive on Tuesday or something like that.

cards.answerEn: it (in the fixed apology lo siento, I'm sorry)

cards.noteEn: Use this fixed expression for an apology or when reacting sympathetically to bad news. Learn it as a complete expression instead of translating lo and siento separately.
cards.questionEn: What is the standard way to say “I'm sorry” when apologizing or expressing sympathy?

example.en: I'm sorry. It was a mistake.

cards.answerEn: I feel (in lo siento: I'm sorry)
I must; I conclude (making an inference)
cards.noteEn: Before haber and a completed-action form, debo can express a strong conclusion about the past rather than a duty. Context distinguishes this from debo followed by an ordinary action, which commonly states an obligation.

example.es: Debo haber dejado la llave dentro.
example.en: I must have left the key inside.

cards.questionEn: How do you make a strong guess about what happened in the past?
cards.answerEn: Use a present form of deber, then haber, then the completed-action form of the main verb.
cards.noteEn: The plus signs show the order of the three pieces. Haber stays unchanged. The final piece is a participle, a completed-action form often ending in -ado or -ido: olvidar becomes olvidado. Deber changes for the person making the inferred action. This use expresses a conclusion, not the obligation commonly expressed by deber plus an ordinary action verb.

example.en: He or she must have forgotten the key.

cards.answerEn: to have, with me attached for the speaker
cards.noteEn: Haberme combines the unchanged helper haber with me. A completed-action form follows it, and me belongs to that following action: haberme equivocado, haberme levantado, or haberme olvidado.

example.en: I may have become confused.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to an action that was already completed after another verb such as poder, deber, or parecer?
cards.answerEn: Use the unchanged helper haber followed by the completed-action form of the main verb.
cards.noteEn: The completed-action form is often called a participle: terminar becomes terminado, hacer becomes hecho, and ser becomes sido. After another verb, haber stays unchanged. The plus sign in the prompt means “followed by.”

example.en: It seems to have ended.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

example.en: I want to help you.

cards.answerEn: some; some day/time (before a masculine noun)
cards.noteEn: Alguno shortens to algún directly before a masculine singular noun: algún día, algún libro.

example.en: Some neighbor will have the key.

cards.answerEn: in; within (a stated period of time)
cards.noteEn: After un momento, de can introduce the larger stretch of time in which that moment falls. Natural English often uses “in” rather than a literal “of.”

example.es: Ocurrió en algún momento de la última semana.
example.en: It happened sometime in the last week.

cards.noteEn: Standard Spanish uses the long scale: un billón is a million million, 10¹². English billion normally means 10⁹, which standard Spanish calls mil millones. English influence can produce nonstandard uses, so the surrounding source matters.

example.es: Un billón es un millón de millones.
example.en: One Spanish billón is a million million (10¹²).

cards.noteEn: Ah can show that the speaker has just understood, noticed, or recognized something. Its exact English equivalent depends on tone.

example.en: Oh, yes, now I remember.

cards.answerEn: you thought; you were thinking (informal singular)
cards.noteEn: Pensabas is the imperfect past form of pensar used for tú. The imperfect presents the thought as an ongoing past viewpoint or background assumption.

example.en: You thought it was Monday.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone finds something easy, difficult, strange, or similar?
cards.answerEn: Name the thing, add me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person, then use a form of resultar and a describing word.
cards.noteEn: The thing being judged controls the form of resultar: la tarea me resulta fácil, las tareas me resultan fáciles. The short word before resultar identifies the person who experiences the judgment. English often makes that person the subject and says “I find...” or “it seems... to me.” An adjective is a word such as fácil or extraño that describes the thing.

example.en: We find these instructions clear.

cards.answerEn: morning; held in the morning (feminine singular)
to you; marks you as the person who finds something a certain way
cards.noteEn: With resultar plus a description, te identifies one familiar person who experiences that impression. The thing producing the impression is the grammatical subject.

example.en: Do you find the task difficult?

cards.noteEn: Resultaban is the imperfect past form of resultar used for a plural subject. With te, it describes how those things seemed or felt to one familiar person.

example.en: The instructions seemed clear to you.
